prompt: What is a portrait mainly intended to represent?
rationale: A portrait depicts a person, whether real or imagined, not necessarily a photographic likeness.

prompt: What is a self-portrait?
answers: An artist's portrait of somebody else
rationale: A self-portrait represents its own maker and need not be a photograph.

prompt: Which painting genre focuses on scenery such as fields, hills and trees?
rationale: Landscape represents natural scenery; it can also include buildings and people.

prompt: What is the main subject of a seascape?
rationale: Seascapes depict marine/coastal scenery.

prompt: What does a cityscape principally show?
answers: A close-up of a single flower
A view of the open sea
rationale: A cityscape represents the appearance of a city or urban area.

prompt: Which description best fits a wholly non-representational abstract painting?
answers: It uses shapes and colours without depicting recognisable objects
It must copy a photograph exactly
It must show a named historical battle
It can only be painted in black
rationale: The explicit non-representational qualifier avoids claiming all abstraction lacks references to real subjects.

prompt: In art, what does figurative usually mean?
answers: Representing recognisable subjects from the real world
rationale: Figurative art retains recognisable representation, rather than necessarily containing human figures alone.

prompt: A face shown in profile is seen from which direction?
rationale: Profile shows a side view of the face.

prompt: In a portrait, what does a full-face view show?
answers: Only the back of the head
Only the outline of a shoulder
rationale: Full-face denotes a frontal view, not necessarily a full-length body portrait.

prompt: Which parts of a person are usually shown in a sculpted bust?
answers: The head, shoulders and upper chest
The entire body from head to foot
rationale: A bust represents the head and upper torso, rather than a full figure.

prompt: What is a silhouette?
answers: A solid shape showing the outline of a subject
A picture made only from written words
rationale: Silhouettes commonly present a dark filled shape against a lighter background.

prompt: In a landscape picture, which area appears closest to the viewer?
rationale: Foreground is the nearest represented space, not necessarily the lower edge in every composition.

prompt: What is the background in a picture?
answers: The area appearing behind the main subject
The nearest object in every picture
The wooden frame around the picture
rationale: Background is the depicted space behind the main subject or nearer forms.

prompt: In a view across open water, what does the horizon line appear to mark?
answers: Where the water meets the sky
The edge of the picture frame
rationale: An open-water horizon appears to separate sea and sky; it is an apparent boundary.

prompt: What is a focal point in an artwork?
answers: An area that particularly draws attention
The label giving the ticket price
rationale: A focal point attracts attention through composition or contrast, not a physical gallery label.

prompt: What is bilateral symmetry in a design?
answers: Two halves reflecting each other across a line
Every shape having a different colour
All objects placed in one corner
rationale: Bilateral symmetry makes mirror-related halves across an axis.

prompt: Which term describes a composition whose two sides are not mirror images?
rationale: Asymmetry lacks mirror matching; it can still have visual balance.

prompt: In art, what does composition mean?
answers: How the elements of the work are arranged
Only the price of the materials
The number of visitors to a gallery
rationale: Composition concerns arrangement of the elements within the artwork.

prompt: What is negative space in a picture?
answers: Space around and between the main shapes
A part that must be removed from the frame
rationale: Negative space surrounds or separates positive forms; it is not a judgment of quality.

prompt: What is linear perspective used to suggest in a flat picture?
answers: The exact age of the canvas
The chemical formula of the pigment
rationale: Linear perspective represents spatial recession through geometric relationships.

prompt: In linear perspective, where do parallel lines receding into the distance appear to meet?
answers: At every corner of the frame
At the lightest colour in the picture
rationale: Receding parallel lines share the appropriate vanishing point for their direction.

prompt: What does a bird's-eye view show?
answers: A subject seen from directly below
Only the inside of a building
Only a close-up of an eye
rationale: The term describes an elevated downward view and does not require birds in the subject.

prompt: What does a worm's-eye view show?
answers: A subject seen from a very low viewpoint
A scene viewed from directly overhead
Only a subject reflected in water
Only a map with no perspective
rationale: A worm-eye view looks from low down, often upwards.

prompt: If one painted object partly hides another, which usually appears nearer?
answers: Both must appear at the same distance
The picture must have no depth
rationale: Occlusion is a familiar depth cue: the covering object usually appears in front.

prompt: What does foreshortening make a form pointing towards the viewer appear?
answers: Always larger than every other object
rationale: Foreshortening represents apparent shortening when a form extends towards or away from the viewer.

prompt: In colour terminology, what does hue identify?
answers: The basic colour family, such as red or blue
How light or dark a colour is
How rough a painted surface feels
rationale: Hue identifies the colour family rather than brightness, size or cost.

prompt: In drawing and painting, what does value refer to?
answers: How light or dark a colour is
Which colour family it belongs to
rationale: Tonal value describes lightness/darkness, not financial value in this context.

prompt: What does colour saturation describe?
answers: The intensity or purity of a colour
The number of objects in a still life
rationale: Saturation distinguishes vivid colours from duller or greyer versions.

prompt: In traditional paint-mixing terminology, how is a tint made?
answers: By adding white to a colour
By adding black to a colour
By mixing only black and grey
rationale: A tint is a colour lightened with white.

prompt: In traditional paint-mixing terminology, how is a shade made?
answers: By adding black to a colour
By adding white to a colour
By mixing only white and grey
rationale: A shade is a colour darkened with black.

prompt: Which pair gives the strongest contrast in lightness?
rationale: Black and white sit at opposite ends of the lightness range; the other pairs have much closer values.

prompt: Where are complementary colours positioned on a traditional colour wheel?
rationale: Complementary hues are opposite on the specified wheel.

prompt: Where are analogous colours found on a colour wheel?
answers: Next to or near each other
Always separated by exactly half the wheel
At the same hue position only
rationale: Analogous schemes use neighbouring hues, unlike complementary opposites.

prompt: What does a monochromatic colour scheme use?
rationale: Monochromatic schemes vary one hue using different values/intensities.

prompt: Which group is traditionally described as warm colours?
rationale: Red through orange and yellow form the conventional warm group.

prompt: Which pair is generally described as cool in basic colour theory?
rationale: Blue and blue-green belong to the conventional cool side of the wheel.

prompt: On the traditional red-yellow-blue paint colour wheel, mixing red and blue gives which secondary colour?
rationale: In the traditional RYB model, red and blue combine to violet/purple; actual pigment mixtures can vary.

prompt: On the traditional red-yellow-blue paint colour wheel, mixing blue and yellow gives which secondary colour?
rationale: In the RYB model, blue and yellow make green.

prompt: Which of these is traditionally classed as a primary paint colour?
rationale: In the traditional red-yellow-blue model used by artists, blue is primary; orange, green and purple are secondary.

prompt: In the traditional red-yellow-blue colour model, a secondary colour is formed by mixing what?
answers: A colour with clear varnish only
rationale: A secondary combines two primaries in the named model.

prompt: Which group contains only achromatic colours?
rationale: Achromatic colours have no hue, unlike the coloured alternatives.

prompt: What type of pigment is ochre?
answers: An earth pigment often yellow or brown
rationale: Ochres are naturally occurring iron-rich earth pigments with yellow/brown/red varieties.

prompt: What is a pastel used for drawing?
answers: A stick of coloured pigment with a binder
A wooden support behind a canvas
A tool used to measure angles
rationale: Pastels supply colour in stick form, with binder types varying between soft, hard and oil pastels.

prompt: Which medium is especially associated with transparent washes over white paper?
rationale: Transparent watercolour washes allow light from the white paper to show through.

prompt: Which of these is commonly used as a binder in artists' oil paint?
rationale: Linseed oil is a common drying-oil binder. Gum arabic is associated with watercolour, egg yolk with tempera and beeswax with encaustic.

prompt: What does impasto mean in painting?
answers: Paint applied thickly enough to leave texture
An outline cut into a printing plate
rationale: Impasto builds up textured paint, often showing brush or knife marks.

prompt: What is a glaze in painting?
answers: A thin transparent layer of paint over another layer
A hole cut through the canvas
rationale: A painted glaze modifies underlying colour through a transparent or translucent layer.

prompt: What is a wash in watercolour painting?
answers: A thin application of diluted colour over an area
A method of cutting the paper into strips
A thick marble base for a statue
A metal plate used only for engraving
rationale: A wash lays diluted colour across an area, evenly or with graduation.

prompt: What is an underpainting?
answers: An initial painted layer beneath later layers
The outside of a picture frame
A painting stored under a table by definition
A title written beneath a sculpture
rationale: Underpainting establishes an early painted structure or tone for later work.

prompt: Which part of paint supplies its colour?
rationale: Pigment provides colour while the binder holds it in a paint film.

prompt: What is the binder in paint used to do?
answers: Evaporate to leave a thinner paint film
rationale: A binder binds the pigment and helps form the paint film.

prompt: What is gesso commonly used for before painting?
answers: Removing every colour from a brush
rationale: Traditional gesso and modern acrylic gesso are preparatory grounds; their ingredients differ.

prompt: What material is a traditional artist's canvas made from?
rationale: Canvas is fabric, often linen or cotton, used as a painting support.

prompt: What is a canvas stretcher?
answers: A framework that holds the canvas taut
A blade used for wood engraving
A varnish used only on frames
rationale: Stretcher bars form an adjustable support framework for stretched canvas.

prompt: What is a sketchbook mainly used to collect?
rationale: A sketchbook holds visual notes and drawings, though artists can also add written notes.

prompt: What is one common purpose of a final varnish on a painting?
answers: To provide a protective surface layer
To change every pigment to white
To turn the canvas into marble
To remove the need for a frame in every case
rationale: A suitable varnish can protect a paint surface and alter its gloss; not every painting is varnished.

prompt: What is a mural?
answers: An artwork painted on a wall or ceiling
A sculpture that must fit in a pocket
rationale: Murals are executed on architectural surfaces such as walls and ceilings.

prompt: Which surface is used for painting in traditional buon fresco?
rationale: Buon fresco applies pigment to fresh wet lime plaster; fresco secco works on dry plaster.

prompt: What is trompe l'oeil intended to do?
answers: Create an illusion that the depicted objects are real
Show only written text with no imagery
Make a sculpture invisible from all sides
rationale: The technique creates a deceptive illusion of three-dimensional reality.

prompt: How many panels make up a diptych?
rationale: A diptych consists of two associated panels.

prompt: How many panels make up a triptych?
rationale: A triptych consists of three associated panels.

prompt: In the phrase panel painting, what is the panel usually made from?
rationale: Panel paintings conventionally use a rigid wooden support.

prompt: What is an illuminated manuscript?
answers: A handwritten book decorated with images or ornament
Any book that can only be read under a lamp
A book made entirely of blank pages
rationale: Illuminated manuscripts combine handwriting with decoration, often including gilding.

prompt: What is calligraphy?
answers: The art of expressive or decorative handwriting
Carving images in wood for printing
Shaping clay into a hollow vessel
rationale: Calligraphy is artistic writing rather than sculpture or flower arranging.

prompt: In a traditional woodcut, which parts of the block usually print the image?
answers: Only the grooves cut below the surface
Only the back of the block
rationale: Woodcut is relief printing: ink on the raised surface transfers to paper while the cut-away areas remain unprinted.

prompt: Which printmaking technique uses a carved sheet of linoleum?
rationale: Linocut uses a sheet of linoleum as the relief block.

prompt: Traditional lithography begins with a design on which kind of surface?
answers: A mesh stretched on a frame
A copper plate with acid-bitten grooves
rationale: Traditional lithography uses a flat limestone surface; modern versions may use plates.

prompt: In screenprinting, ink is pushed through what?
answers: A mesh screen with selected areas blocked
rationale: The stencil blocks parts of a mesh so ink passes only where required.

prompt: In printmaking, what is an edition?
answers: A set of prints produced from the same image
A brush used only for blue paint
A carved border around a frame
The outside wall of a museum
rationale: An edition comprises a set of impressions, often numbered, from the same print image.

prompt: What is a trial proof in printmaking?
answers: A test impression used to check work in progress
A receipt proving a ticket was purchased
The final auction price of a print
A wooden plinth for a sculpture
rationale: Trial proofs let a printmaker assess an image before or between changes.

prompt: What is a relief sculpture?
answers: A sculpture projecting from a background surface
A sculpture that must be suspended by a string
A sculpture made only from transparent glass
A sculpture with no three-dimensional form
rationale: Relief forms remain attached to or rise from a background plane.

prompt: A sculpture in the round is designed to be viewed how?
answers: Only as a flat shadow on paper
Only from inside a closed box
rationale: In-the-round sculpture is fully three-dimensional, unlike relief against a backing.

prompt: In sculpture, what does carving do?
answers: Removes material to create a form
Adds soft material layer by layer only
Prints an image on a flat sheet
rationale: Carving is subtractive, unlike additive modelling.

prompt: In sculpture, what does modelling usually involve?
answers: Shaping and building up a pliable material
Only printing with an inked plate
rationale: Modelling shapes pliable materials such as clay or wax and can build up form.

prompt: What is an armature in sculpture?
answers: An internal framework supporting the material
A final coat of transparent varnish
The title on a picture label
rationale: An armature supports a model or sculpture, often through wire or another framework.

prompt: What is a plinth used for when displaying a sculpture?
answers: Making a print from a plate
rationale: A plinth is a supporting base beneath a sculpture.

prompt: What is a patina on a metal sculpture?
answers: A surface appearance that develops or is deliberately created
The wooden crate used for delivery
The paper label giving its dimensions
The empty space inside the gallery
rationale: Patina is a surface layer or finish arising naturally or through treatment.

prompt: Which of these is a natural stone traditionally used for carving statues?
rationale: Marble is a stone used for carved sculpture; the alternatives are different artistic materials.

prompt: What does site-specific art mean?
answers: Art made with a particular location in mind
Art that must fit on a website
Art that has no intended setting
Art made only from building bricks
rationale: Site-specific work is conceived for the characteristics of a particular place.

prompt: What is installation art especially concerned with?
answers: Arranging elements to create an experience within a space
Painting a likeness of a sitter on one small panel
Printing a run of identical postal labels
Carving letters into a single gravestone
rationale: Installations organise objects, media and space into an artwork or environment.

prompt: In performance art, what is a central part of the artwork?
answers: Actions carried out by the artist or performers
The insurance value of a framed painting
The sales history of a printed book
The mineral composition of a stone plinth
rationale: Performance art is realised through actions, potentially live or recorded.

prompt: In conceptual art, what is often given particular importance?
answers: The weight of the display frame alone
The cost of the paint alone
rationale: Conceptual art prioritises ideas rather than requiring one traditional material or technique.

prompt: What is public art generally intended for?
answers: A setting accessible to the public
Only an artist's locked private cupboard
Only the back of a sealed picture frame
Only a book that nobody may open
rationale: Public art is made for public settings and audiences, not necessarily owned by government.

prompt: What is the main purpose of an art gallery?
answers: Producing canvas for artists to paint on
rationale: Art galleries exhibit artworks; some also sell them.

prompt: Which role typically selects and interprets works for an exhibition?
rationale: Curators select, research and interpret exhibition contents; the other named roles have different primary functions.

prompt: What is an art conservator primarily concerned with?
answers: Setting estimates for an art auction
Making reproductions for a gift shop
rationale: Conservation preserves objects through examination, preventive care and appropriate treatment.

prompt: What does an artwork's provenance describe?
answers: Only the direction of its brushstrokes
Only the width of its frame
rationale: Provenance records ownership and often associated history, rather than merely visual qualities.

prompt: What is a reproduction of a painting?
answers: A copy of the painting's image
A treatment to repair the original surface
A new frame made for the original
An assessment of who made the original
rationale: Reproductions copy the image through printing or other methods.

prompt: What does an exhibition catalogue usually contain?
answers: Information about the works and artists in the exhibition
Only the museum staff work rota
rationale: Exhibition catalogues document the exhibited works and provide related information.

prompt: What is the window mount around a drawing or print?
answers: A cut-out board border surrounding the visible image
A wooden rod used to roll up the picture
A wire framework inside a statue
rationale: A window mount frames the visible image within an opening in mount board.

prompt: Why might a drawing be protected by glass when it is framed?
answers: To help protect it from dust and accidental contact
To make every drawn line physically thicker
To prove the exact year in which it was drawn
To replace all faded pigments automatically
rationale: Glazing offers a physical protective barrier. It does not prove a date or restore faded colour; UV filtering depends on the glazing type.

prompt: On a drawing made on a sheet of paper, recto usually refers to which side?
rationale: Recto denotes the front or principal face of the sheet.

prompt: On a drawing made on a sheet of paper, verso usually refers to which side?
rationale: Verso denotes the reverse of a sheet.

prompt: What information is commonly included on a museum label beside a painting?
answers: The stock numbers of shop souvenirs
rationale: Object labels commonly identify the work, maker, date and medium, with variations for unknown details.

prompt: Why are some light-sensitive drawings displayed under low lighting?
answers: To help limit fading and light damage
To let faded colours restore themselves automatically
To make all paper completely waterproof
To prevent every form of insect damage
rationale: Reducing light exposure helps protect sensitive media and paper; damage can be cumulative.

prompt: What is an artist's portfolio?
answers: A selected collection of their work
Only a list of frame prices
A chemical used to clean brushes
rationale: A portfolio presents selected work and can be physical or digital.

prompt: What is an art commission?
answers: A request for an artist to create a work
Only a free ticket to a museum
rationale: Commissioning arranges creation of a particular work; payment and terms vary.

prompt: What does an artist's statement usually explain?
answers: Ideas and intentions behind their work
Only the weight of the canvas
Only how to replace a printer cartridge
rationale: An artist statement explains aspects of the maker practice, ideas or intentions.

prompt: What does an artist's signature on a work normally identify?
answers: The owner of every later copy
The number of visitors who have seen it
rationale: Signatures identify claimed authorship but do not alone guarantee authenticity.

prompt: In an art catalogue, what does attribution concern?
answers: Who is believed to have made a work
Who owned it at every point in its history
How much its shipping crate weighs
How long visitors must queue to see it
rationale: Attribution identifies or proposes the maker, sometimes with qualifications expressing uncertainty.
